parsed_answer.content:
In modern Spring Boot development, the @SpringBootApplication annotation acts as the primary entry point for bootstrapping applications, encapsulating three foundational meta-annotations: @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration, and @ComponentScan. To truly master enterprise application design, one must understand how these components interact under the hood to configure the ApplicationContext, scan the classpath for components, and trigger intelligent auto-configuration based on conditional bean loading. 

When a Spring Boot application starts, @Configuration designates the main class as a source of bean definitions, allowing it to contain @Bean methods that are processed by the IoC container. Concurrently, @ComponentScan instructs the container to search designated packages for classes annotated with stereotypes like @Component, @Service, @Repository, and @Controller, registering them automatically into the bean factory. Finally, @EnableAutoConfiguration leverages the SpringFactoriesLoader mechanism to inspect the classpath for third-party libraries—such as Jackson, Hibernate, or embedded Tomcat—and conditionally instantiate the infrastructure beans required to make those libraries work out of the box.

rows: Marks class as a bean definition source
Triggers conditional configuration via classpath scanning

items: The @Configuration annotation operates by generating a runtime CGLIB proxy of the configuration class, intercepting bean method invocations to ensure singleton semantics are preserved across inter-bean dependencies.

@ComponentScan defaults to scanning the package of the annotated class and its sub-packages, which dictates why placing the main class in the root package is a strict convention for avoiding unindexed components.

@EnableAutoConfiguration reads the META-INF/spring.factories file (or modern org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports files) to load hundreds of auto-configuration candidate classes safely guarded by conditional annotations like @ConditionalOnClass and @ConditionalOnMissingBean.

parsed_answer.content: A common production trap for senior engineers is placing the @SpringBootApplication main class in a utility package instead of the root package (e.g., com.enterprise.util instead of com.enterprise). Because @ComponentScan defaults to the package of the annotated class, placing it too deep causes Spring Boot to silently miss domain components, resulting in NoSuchBeanDefinitionException errors at runtime.
